candidates.statement: 23 Section 506(c)(1)(A) of the FD&C Act requires FDA to consider the availability or lack of alternative treatments in determining whether a product should be approved under accelerated approval. Additionally, FDA’s accelerated approval regulations state that accelerated approval is available only for drugs that provide a meaningful therapeutic benefit to patients over existing treatments (21 CFR 314.500; 601.40). FDA has generally interpreted these requirements to mean that accelerated approval is only available for products that address an unmet medical need.

candidates.statement: A surrogate endpoint is generally a biomarker, such as a laboratory measurement, radiographic 193 image, physical sign, or other measure, that is thought to predict clinical benefit but is not itself a 194 measure of clinical benefit. In general, depending on the strength of the evidence supporting the 195 ability of a biomarker to predict clinical benefit, the biomarker may be (1) a surrogate endpoint 196 that is known to predict clinical benefit (i.e., a validated surrogate endpoint that could be used for 197 traditional approval); (2) a surrogate endpoint that is reasonably likely to predict a drug’s 198 intended clinical benefit (i.e., a reasonably likely surrogate endpoint that could be the basis for 199 accelerated approval); or (3) a biomarker for which there is insufficient evidence to support 200 reliance on the biomarker as either kind of surrogate endpoint (i.e., an endpoint that cannot be 201 used to support accelerated or traditional approval of a marketing application). 26 There are many 202 serious diseases with an unmet medical need for which available biomarkers lack the necessary 203 evidence to support a conclusion that they are reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit. Such 204 biomarkers are not suitable to support either accelerated or traditional approval. In these cases, 205 sponsors should consult with the appropriate review division regarding the path forward. 206

In making the judgment as to whether a drug’s effect on a given endpoint is reasonably likely to 302 predict clinical benefit, FDA considers all relevant evidence and may consult external experts, 303 including through consulting advisory committees, as needed and as permitted by law. This 304 guidance provides an overview of some of the important factors to consider in identifying and 305 assessing whether surrogate endpoints or intermediate clinical endpoints are reasonably likely to 306 predict clinical benefit. This guidance does not, however, address the specific clinical evidence 307 needed to support a conclusion that a particular surrogate endpoint or intermediate clinical 308 endpoint is reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit, because such evidence is case-specific 309 and is not readily generalizable. 310

candidates.context: There are also cases in which, rather than using a clinical endpoint to provide persuasive 424 evidence of clinical benefit, it may be appropriate to use additional evaluation (i.e., longer trial 425 duration) of the same surrogate endpoint that was used to support accelerated approval in the 426 same population. For example, historically, in HIV treatment, an effect on viral load of 427 relatively short duration (24 weeks) was considered reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit, 428 supporting accelerated approval. However, an effect of longer (48 weeks) viral load suppression 429 was more convincingly related to durable clinical benefit in the setting of lifelong therapy and 430 thus was used to verify clinical benefit. candidates.statement: The Agency generally expects that any proposal to withdraw approval of a drug that has been 545 granted accelerated approval will be issued by the center or centers (hereafter, Center) that 546 approved the drug. When the data or other information received by the Agency raises concerns 547 that one or more of the criteria for withdrawing approval may have been met, responsible 548 officials within the Center should discuss their concerns with the sponsor and seek an appropriate 549 resolution. Such discussions may result in the sponsor’s voluntary request for withdrawal of 550 approval under 21 CFR 314.150 or 21 CFR 601.5(a) or other regulatory actions, as appropriate, 551 depending on the circumstances. 552
